cells.tense: Right now the feeling and the shape are working together in your hands.
cells.act: keep the motivation warm with steady care
cells.ask: Tomorrow, go back to what you're building and read it again — notice what it asks for, and do only that piece. Ten minutes.
cells.core:
You meet what's unshaped with fresh attention — a new project, a mood with no name yet — and a form comes out of that contact: you sense what's alive in it, then you build something that holds it. What you make keeps working because the structure grew from the thing rather than being laid over it.

When you sense the shape is right, stay a little past the point that feels finished. You're quick to notice and quick to build, and you can leave before the last layer sets. Tending the thing after the spark — watering it, checking what it still needs — is the same feeling carried further, the fire warm instead of smothered. What you build then lasts past the first week, and the building costs you less than you thought.

cells.tense: You're sketching the whole structure before the feeling has shown you what it needs.
cells.act: care for it with fresh hands and see what it needs
cells.ask: Set down what you're about to build for a week. Each day, tend something small and growing, and look before you do anything else.
cells.core:
Before anything has shown itself, you've drafted the structure: the plan, the calendar, the shape of how the whole thing should go. You're reading the situation a season beyond where it actually is, and the feeling hasn't caught up. What you build comes down before it can respond to anything, and the people in it get tired of rearranging the scaffolding.

Go back to something small and living — a plant, a page, a routine — and tend it the way a beginner would: water it when it's dry, move it toward the light, watch what it actually does. You don't have to know how it grows; you learn by keeping it. Then the structures you build come up from something already breathing, and you stop working past the thing you're holding.

cells.tense: You're still on the other side of a door that's already opened and closed.
cells.act: follow a raw curiosity with no use for it
cells.ask: Chase one curiosity this week with no plan and no purpose — read the piece, ask the question, keep going a little past where you meant to stop.
cells.core:
You once went into things wide open, and somewhere along the way the openness stopped arriving. Now you watch a situation from a comfortable distance — you can describe it accurately, even plan for it — but you don't lean into it with fresh attention, so no structure gets built from the inside. Abstract demands you can handle; the concrete making feels stalled.

When order and details crowd out exploring, curiosity goes dormant. Set the question you're already carrying next to how you'd examine it with a friend in mind, and stop making the answer do all the work. Attention returns without being pushed, and the structure comes back with it.

cells.tense: You're reading the room's shape and calling it weather that just happened to you.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Write what happened in order — the facts, no feeling words, a page. Read it back and ask whose eyes it was written from.
cells.core:
You walk into a situation and within minutes you know how it runs, what the mood is, where it will get bumpy. You talk about that shape as if it were simply there — something you found rather than something you have been quietly making as you enter. What you understand about how a room works is original, and you aren't counting it as yours.

Before you were arranging anything, you were someone who looked closely and put down what you saw. Write a page of it plainly, without feeling words, and read it back to yourself. The observation is yours, and the one who wrote it is the one who will shape what comes next.
